intro: Le Porge is a village in the pine forests of the Médoc in Gironde, a few kilometres in from the Atlantic dunes. On Place Saint-Seurin, beside the long south wall of its stone church, stands a tall plane tree with a pale mottled trunk that forks high above the roof. A reader sent us its photograph and tells us it was planted in the late nineteenth century.

question_answer: The Plane Tree of Place Saint-Seurin stands on the grass beside the south wall of the Église Saint-Seurin, on the village square of Le Porge in Gironde. It is free to visit at any hour.
question_context: A reader sent us this plane tree from Le Porge, a village in the pine country of the Médoc, a few kilometres from the Atlantic coast of Gironde. It stands on the grass of Place Saint-Seurin, against the long side wall of the Église Saint-Seurin, the church on the old pilgrim road to Santiago. In the reader's photograph the trunk rises straight and pale, flaking in grey, cream and olive patches, before forking high above the church roof into two great stems; a person at its foot reaches barely a fifth of the way to the fork. The reader tells us it was planted in the late nineteenth century, which would make it about 145 years old, and that it was recognised as a Remarkable Tree of France in 2003. We have not yet found that label in a source, so we state it as theirs and ask anyone who knows the village's record to tell us. The square is public and open at all hours.

trees.story:
Le Porge is a village in the pine country of the Médoc, a few kilometres in from the Atlantic dunes, and on its square, against the long side wall of the Église Saint-Seurin, stands this plane. A reader sent us its photograph from the foot of the trunk.

The picture shows why they stopped. The trunk rises straight and pale, flaking in the camouflage patches of grey, cream and olive that planes are known for, then forks high above the church roof into two great stems that spread a crown wider than the nave. The person standing at its foot reaches barely a fifth of the way to the fork. The church spire, in the same pale stone, rises behind it.

The reader tells us it was planted in the late nineteenth century, which would make it about 145 years old, and that it was recognised as a Remarkable Tree of France in 2003. Those facts are theirs: we have not yet found the label in a source, and if you know the village's record of this tree, tell us here and we will add it.

Stand on the grass by the church wall and look straight up the trunk to the fork.
